title: How Pirates Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and mechanics of piracy, from ancient and medieval seafaring raiders through the Barbary pirates, the Golden Age of piracy (c. 1690-1730) with figures like Blackbeard, Calico Jack, Anne Bonny and Mary Read, and the Whydah wreck. They cover privateers and letters of mark, pirate life and punishments, the Jolly Roger, boarding tactics, the myths of walking the plank and peg legs, and modern piracy in the Gulf of Aden fueled by Somali pirates, ransom kidnappings, and anti-piracy measures. The episode closes with a listener email from Danny, who was a baby used as a hostage shield in a Queens standoff. Note: the transcript is an auto-style transcription with errors in names and numbers.

segments.title: Opening banter and pirate definition
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter about pirate-themed episode and Talk Like a Pirate Day, then define a pirate as someone using a private vessel to attack another boat for private gain outside government authority.

segments.title: Privateers and why piracy arises
segments.summary: Privateers held government letters of mark and often turned to piracy during peacetime. Economic hardship and rich trade routes both drove piracy throughout history.

segments.title: Early and regional piracy history
segments.summary: Piracy is traced to at least the fourth century BC, with raids off Turkey in the fourteenth century, Corsairs and Barbary pirates in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, and Chinese piracy after the Han dynasty. The buccaneers gave the Tampa Bay team its name.

segments.title: Pirate stereotypes and the Golden Age
segments.summary: The hosts discuss popular pirate imagery such as tricorn hats, hoop earrings, parrots, peg legs and Johnny Depp, then describe the Golden Age of piracy from about 1690 to 1730.

segments.title: Blackbeard, Calico Jack, Anne Bonny and Mary Read
segments.summary: Calico Jack allowed women pirates. Anne Bonny and Mary Read sailed aboard his ship, disguising themselves as women or men depending on the situation, and a witness said they cursed with the best of the crew.

segments.title: Trade winds, slavery and pirate treasure
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a theory that trade winds shaped the Atlantic slave trade, then describe pirates typically seizing sugar, rum and molasses rather than gold, with the Whydah sinking in 1717 off Cape Cod as an exception carrying gold and jewels.

segments.title: Pirate flags, recruitment and marooning
segments.summary: Pirates flew false colors to intimidate, and the Jolly Roger sometimes showed a skeleton. Crews were often recruited from captives, who were given the choice to join, be shot, or be marooned on an island.

segments.title: Pirate clothing, weapons and myths
segments.summary: The hosts separate pirate myths from fact: flintlock pistols were used despite saltwater problems, peg legs and hooks were plausible due to gunpowder injuries, while walking the plank and parrots as pirate fixtures are fiction from books like Treasure Island and Peter Pan.

segments.title: Life at sea, boarding tactics and punishments
segments.summary: Pirates ate hardtack and spoiled meat, boarded at night using grappling hooks from the stern, disabled rudders, used grapeshot against the helmsman, and punished captives or crew with keelhauling and bottle-throwing. Ships also cleaned barnacles to gain speed.

segments.title: Modern piracy in the Gulf of Aden
segments.summary: Modern piracy has returned, driven by economic hardship, underreporting, and Somalia's lack of a functioning government. The Gulf of Aden is a bottleneck for oil and goods, and modern pirates use RPGs, machine guns, and ransom holds on ships.

segments.title: Anti-piracy advice for ships
segments.summary: The hosts offer advice for ships facing pirates: keep route plans quiet in port, keep watch, search for stowaways, call for help, sound alarms and lights, use fire hoses, and consider electrified deck fencing.

segments.title: Listener mail: hostage shield story
segments.summary: Listener Danny recounts being a baby held by his father during a Queens standoff, where police used negotiators and a priest to end it. The hosts discuss human shields in hostage situations.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listener emails, point to the HowStuffWorks site for more on pirates, and close the show.
